1	# gatsby-plugin-google-tagmanager
2	
3	Easily add Google Tagmanager to your Gatsby site.
4	
5	## Install
6	
7	`npm install --save gatsby-plugin-google-tagmanager`
8	
9	## How to use
10	
11	```javascript
12	// In your gatsby-config.js
13	plugins: [
14	  {
15	    resolve: `gatsby-plugin-google-tagmanager`,
16	    options: {
17	      id: "YOUR_GOOGLE_TAGMANAGER_ID",
18	
19	      // Include GTM in development.
20	      // Defaults to false meaning GTM will only be loaded in production.
21	      includeInDevelopment: false,
22	
23	      // Specify optional GTM environment details.
24	      gtmAuth: "YOUR_GOOGLE_TAGMANAGER_ENVIRONMENT_AUTH_STRING",
25	      gtmPreview: "YOUR_GOOGLE_TAGMANAGER_ENVIRONMENT_PREVIEW_NAME",
26	      dataLayerName: "YOUR_DATA_LAYER_NAME",
27	    },
28	  },
29	]
30	```
31	
32	#### Tracking routes
33	
34	This plugin will fire a new event called `gatsby-route-change` whenever a route is changed in your Gatsby application. To record this in Google Tag Manager, we will need to add a trigger to the desired tag to listen for the event:
35	
36	1. Visit the [Google Tag Manager console](https://tagmanager.google.com/) and click on the workspace for your site.
37	2. Navigate to the desired tag using the 'Tags' tab of the menu on the right hand side.
38	3. Under "Triggering", click the pencil icon, then the "+" button to add a new trigger.
39	4. In the "Choose a trigger" window, click on the "+" button again.
40	5. Choose the trigger type by clicking the pencil button and clicking "Custom event". For event name, enter `gatsby-route-change`.
41	
42	This tag will now catch every route change in Gatsby, and you can add Google tag services as you wish to it.
43	
44	#### Note
45	
46	Out of the box this plugin will simply load Google Tag Manager on the initial page/app load. It's up to you to fire tags based on changes in your app. See the above "Tracking routes" section for an example.

Here's what I found about the `gatsby-plugin-google-tagmanager` plugin's `onRenderBody` implementation and the `reporter.panic` behavior related to `defaultDataLayer` in `gatsby-ssr.js`.

## How `onRenderBody` works in `gatsby-ssr.js`

The plugin's server-side rendering hook is where GTM scripts get injected into your HTML. The `exports.onRenderBody` function receives `{ setHeadComponents, setPreBodyComponents, reporter }` along with plugin options including `id`, `includeInDevelopment` (default false), `gtmAuth`, `gtmPreview`, `defaultDataLayer`, `dataLayerName` (default "dataLayer"), `enableWebVitalsTracking` (default false), and `selfHostedOrigin` (default "https://www.googletagmanager.com").

The GTM scripts are only injected under certain conditions — the logic runs if `process.env.NODE_ENV === "production"` OR if `includeInDevelopment` is set. This is why GTM typically doesn't appear during local development unless you explicitly enable it.

## The `reporter.panic` and `defaultDataLayer` validation

The plugin validates the `defaultDataLayer` option and will halt the build if it isn't a plain object. The code calls `reporter.panic` with the message that the plugin option "defaultDataLayer" should be a plain object, indicating the provided value "is not valid."

Internally, when a `defaultDataLayer` is provided, `onRenderBody` calls `generateDefaultDataLayer(defaultDataLayer, reporter, dataLayerName)` to produce the data layer code. That helper builds the output like this: `window.${dataLayerName}.push(...)` is appended after checking validity, and the result is returned via `stripIndent`.

## Why `reporter.panic` fires

The validation was introduced to reject invalid data layer values. From the original PR that added this behavior, the tests confirm the intent: with `pluginOptions` such as `defaultDataLayer: { type: "number", value: 5 }` or a class instance (`new Test()`), calling `onRenderBody(mocks, pluginOptions)` is expected to throw. In those tests, the mock `reporter` is defined with `panic: msg => { throw new Error(msg) }`, so a panic effectively throws and stops the build.

## Correct usage of `defaultDataLayer`

To avoid the panic, `defaultDataLayer` must be a plain object or a function returning one. Per the official docs: the data layer to be set before GTM is loaded should be an object or a function that is executed in the browser, and it defaults to null — for example `defaultDataLayer: { platform: "gatsby" }`.

If you need runtime/browser data, use the function form: `defaultDataLayer: function () { return { pageType: window.pageType } }`.

According to the TypeScript type definitions, the accepted shape is: `defaultDataLayer` is the data layer to be set before Google Tag Manager is loaded and should be an object or a function (default null), typed as `object | (() => object) | null`.

## Summary / How to fix

If you're hitting `reporter.panic` with the "defaultDataLayer should be a plain object" message, check your `gatsby-config.js`:
- **Valid:** a plain object literal (`{ platform: "gatsby" }`) or a function returning a plain object.
- **Invalid (causes panic):** primitives like numbers/strings, or non-plain objects such as class instances.

One related historical caveat worth noting: a past release introduced a bug where the default `dataLayer` was set as `datalayer` (all lowercase), which meant it wouldn't work with GTM by default. If you're on an older version, ensure `dataLayerName` resolves correctly to `dataLayer`.

You can view the full current source directly in the [Gatsby GitHub repo](https://github.com/gatsbyjs/gatsby/blob/master/packages/gatsby-plugin-google-tagmanager/src/gatsby-ssr.js) for the exact implementation.
